Edition note: An independent English rewriting for English-language readers, preserving the Chinese argument while reorganizing context, sequence, and emphasis. Full-series spoilers.

More than the dirty joke

Samantha Jones is often remembered as the woman supplying the loudest, most sexually explicit line at the table. Her dialogue becomes a meme, a quotation, or evidence of the show's daring. None of that is entirely wrong. It can, however, obscure a more consequential feature: among the four friends, she is especially persistent about refusing to let other people's standards define her life.

Carrie has her column and an audience, as well as her long uncertainty about Big. Charlotte has assembled a recognizable picture of a good life. Miranda's independence often takes the negative form of refusing to be the kind of woman who needs a man, which still defines a position against something else. Samantha is more willing to begin with what she wants, without consulting someone else's timetable or preparing a defense.

When her sexual life becomes an object of curiosity, concern, or judgment at brunch, she does not always accept the offered measuring stick. Enjoyment need not produce a debt of explanation. Rather than win every argument about whether her life is acceptable, she can decline the premise that it requires an external verdict.

She does not manage that refusal flawlessly on every occasion. Its significance is as a persistent line of judgment, not proof of invulnerability. The line is more interesting than any individual joke.

A position that does not need curing

It is a mistake to interpret Samantha's entire life as avoidance of intimacy, with every pleasure a symptom awaiting the right man's cure. She can be frightened and retreat. Richard's declarations of love are not easy for her to answer. That does not make her previous choices an illness.

Her position contains three substantial claims. Sex can be good in itself, without requiring some additional promise to justify it. A long-term relationship is not a compulsory component of a complete life. And wanting something is a reason to say so directly rather than turn desire into hints, tests, and indirection.

Experience tests all three claims; it does not simply invalidate them. They can protect her because another person's judgment is not automatically translated into her own worth. Rejection may hurt without meaning she is inadequate. There can be a boundary between being sad and rewriting the self around someone else's refusal.

Richard Wright exposes the limits of that protection. Their relationship begins in the fourth season with a degree of compatibility: he is intelligent, wealthy, and initially seems to understand relationships much as she does. She falls in love. After discovering his betrayal, she tries to trust him again, but reconciliation does not stop suspicion.

In the fifth season, at an Atlantic City hotel, she finds herself climbing stairs to check on him. Her days are becoming a surveillance operation. Leaving is not simply a verdict on whether he loves her. She refuses the person she is becoming while she waits for the next injury. She already tells Richard that she loves herself more. The later repetition matters because the circumstances will be much harder to judge.

Smith

Smith Jerrod enters as a strikingly handsome young waiter who wants to act. Samantha initially notices the looks. Their relationship develops into something stronger partly because he does not demand a replacement version of her. Her age, income, history, and outspoken manner are not defects he sets out to correct.

He is also becoming someone in his own right. Samantha uses her professional abilities to help turn an aspiring actor into a star. She is good at this work, and her investment is not merely a way to possess him. She sees something worth developing. The support she gives resembles the freedom she wants for herself: let me be who I am, and help me do it better.

That reciprocity makes their relationship more than a story in which a younger man finally domesticates a woman who has been excessive. Love adds a person and a shared undertaking to her life. It need not begin by declaring her earlier self deficient.

The wig

In the sixth season, Samantha is diagnosed with breast cancer. Chemotherapy brings hair loss and other bodily changes. She continues to work, pursue clients, seek information, and manage treatment with the determination she brings to professional problems. A wig helps preserve the recognizable, polished Samantha Jones. Illness is not allowed to supply her entire identity.

But refusing to be reduced to illness can become confused with refusing to acknowledge one's actual situation. At a breast-cancer benefit luncheon, she begins with a prepared speech. Then the hot flashes become intolerable. She abandons the decorous script, speaks about what her body is undergoing, and removes her wig. Other women in the audience remove theirs too.

The scene's force is not exhausted by calling her brave. The wig was intended to let her continue being herself, the glamorous woman who appeared in control. At this point, maintaining that image has begun to keep her outside her own experience. People before her share the discomfort. A flawless appearance is no longer the only way to meet them.

Removing the wig does not mean that image never matters. It means refusing an image that can no longer hold the person. Charlotte's previous essay described changing the container rather than abandoning the desire. Here a very different woman performs a related act: the familiar outward form must yield because it has become too small.

Smith's gesture belongs beside it. He shaves his own head in front of her. For an actor, hair is part of the professional appearance too. His response is not merely to reassure her from outside the change, but to enter some of its visibility with her. Samantha learns something about allowing care at the very moment she cannot secure herself through an immaculate presentation.

Loving herself more

In the first film, Samantha is in Los Angeles with Smith. She manages his schedule and career, accompanies him to public events, and waits for work to end. Her own days increasingly revolve around his. She eats more, watches an attractive neighbor, and becomes dissatisfied with the shape of her life.

Smith still loves her. There is no newly discovered betrayal that can settle the matter on her behalf. When she leaves, she says she has tried: she has given the relationship five years and fifteen pounds. She loves him, but loves herself more.

Detached from the story, the line can sound like a declaration requiring no argument. In fact, its weight lies in its repetition. She has said it to Richard before. Leaving him meant refusing to continue organizing her life around his betrayal and her suspicion. Leaving Smith means leaving someone who shaved his head, stood beside her through cancer, and remains one of the kindest partners in the series.

This is not the same as discovering that a seemingly good relationship was secretly evil all along. The question is whether she wants to remain the person her current life is making her. A partner's goodness cannot answer that question for her. Love can remain real while a shared arrangement becomes unlivable.

Across both departures, the criterion persists, while its application grows more difficult. Samantha has learned to love, to accept care, and to stop pretending when she is vulnerable. None of those developments requires her to abandon the authority to judge her own life. She takes that judgment into a genuine love and uses it when a decision is needed.

The relevant measure of a relationship cannot be only whether the other person has committed an offense. It must also include who one is becoming inside it. That is a useful question about a bad relationship. About a good one, it is harder, and more necessary, to ask.

Sex and the City, created by Darren Star, aired from 1998 to 2004 across six seasons and ninety-four episodes, followed by films in 2008 and 2010.
